# JOLT Atlas

JOLT Atlas is a zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) framework that extends the JOLT proving system to support ML inference verification from ONNX models.

Made with ❤️ by ICME Labs.

## Overview

JOLT Atlas enables practical zero-knowledge machine learning by leveraging Just One Lookup Table (JOLT) technology. Traditional circuit-based approaches are prohibitively expensive when representing non-linear functions like ReLU and SoftMax. Lookups eliminate the need for circuit representation entirely.

In JOLT Atlas, we eliminate the complexity that plagues other approaches: no quotient polynomials, no byte decomposition, no grand products, no permutation checks, and most importantly — no complicated circuits.

## Verify a release

None of these use the GitHub API, which is rate limited and which Atlas clients do not call either:
    
    # What GitHub shows as "Latest": the newest build of the default channel (an alpha pre-GA), NOT the Stable channel
    curl -sI https://github.com/codeatlasdev/atlas/releases/latest | grep -i '^location:'
    
    # Stable, beta and alpha: the feed clients read, newest first (Stable = the newest tag with no prerelease label;
    # older entries: releases.atom?after=<oldest tag shown>)
    curl -fsSL https://github.com/codeatlasdev/atlas/releases.atom | grep -o '<title>[^<]*</title>' | head
    
    # The assets and what each channel offers right now, as the clients compute it
    curl -fsSIL https://github.com/codeatlasdev/atlas/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/manifest.json | head -1
    atlas update channel --json
    atlas update --check

Check the checksums of a download:
    
    curl -fsSLO https://github.com/codeatlasdev/atlas/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/SHA256SUMS
    shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

Users get the new version with `atlas update`, which downloads `atlas-<version>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` from the release and then the matching `Atlas-<version>-…app.tar.gz` when Atlas Desktop is installed. Or they click Update CLI & app in the app. Check the app asset with `atlas desktop --install --latest --no-open && atlas desktop --status`.

## Yanking a bad release

A release that must not be installed is handled in the open and never rewritten:

  1. Mark it in `CHANGELOG.md`: `## [1.4.0-beta.2] — 2026-10-20 [YANKED]` with one line saying why and which version to use instead. Do not delete the section.
  2. Ship the fix as the next version (`beta.3`, or `patch` for a stable). Clients move up to it by SemVer precedence.
  3. Only the maintainer may then demote or remove the GitHub release: `gh release edit vX.Y.Z --prerelease` (a release stops being "Latest" once something newer is marked latest; demoting a default-channel alpha hands "Latest" back to the previous build only when you also `gh release edit <tag> --latest`), or `gh release delete vX.Y.Z` for a build that is dangerous to keep downloadable. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1.5.0-alpha.23 Alpha

October 26, 2026Release page and downloads

Atlas is in alpha: expect bugs and breaking changes. Please report what breaks.

### Fixed

  * Linux: much less work per terminal while agents stream output (the likely cause of "one tab lags, two freeze the app"; please report how it behaves on your machine). Terminal output reached the webview as one script evaluation per hostd chunk (dozens a second per terminal, each a round trip into WebKitGTK); it is now one event per terminal per frame. Each terminal also registered its own listeners for host events (two IPC calls and a callback per hostd event, per terminal); the page now has one listener per event name, routed by terminal. And an xterm.js terminal that is fed faster than it can parse (a build log, `cat` of a big file, an agent redrawing a full screen 30 times a second on a slow webview) no longer queues up to 50 MB: past 4 MiB it drops the rest and redraws from the host's replay once it has caught up.
  * Linux: the main window is no longer an alpha window. The page paints an opaque background there, so the transparency (needed only for macOS vibrancy) only made WebKitGTK and the compositor blend the whole window every frame.

### Added

  * Linux: the graphics setup is in the app log. Session type, display servers, NVIDIA driver and every `WEBKIT_`, `GDK_`, `GSK_` variable set are written once at startup (`~/.atlas/desktop/app.log`, and so in "Copy diagnostics"); Troubleshooting lists the three variables to try, in order.

Atlas is in alpha: expect bugs and breaking changes. Please report what breaks.
Agent instances get their own WebKit store (`atlas desktop --agent --gc` cleans leftovers). See `docs/contributing.md`.
  * For contributors: live mirror of an agent instance. `bun run desktop:mirror` shows the instance's whole window (GPU terminal included) at about 30 fps in your browser, and forwards your clicks and keys; nothing appears on your screen.

Atlas is in alpha: expect bugs and breaking changes. Please report what breaks.

### Added

  * Atlas on Linux. Releases now ship Linux x86_64 builds of the CLI and Atlas Desktop: `install.sh` and `atlas update` work on Linux, `atlas desktop` installs the AppImage to `~/.local/bin/atlas-desktop` with a menu entry, and every release has an Arch package (`sudo pacman -U codeatlas-atlas-bin-*.pkg.tar.zst`, plus its `PKGBUILD`), a `.deb`, an `.rpm` and an AppImage, each with both `atlas` and `atlas-desktop`. After folding, an ordinary matmul is just a degree-2 dot product over the contraction cube; batch matmul over attention heads rides one `EqSchedule` inside that single sum-check rather than looping per head. The initial claim is the fused-rebase reconstruction, not the output opening:
    
    `pub fn fused_input_claim<F: JoltField>(...) -> F {
        match rebase_bits(&node.operator) {
            Some(bits) if bits > 0 => {
                let rescaled = accessor.get_advice(VirtualPoly::ClampAcc).1;
                let remainder = accessor.get_advice(VirtualPoly::RescaleRemainder).1;
                rescaled * F::from_u64(1u64 << bits) + remainder
            }
            _ => accessor.get_reduced_opening().1,
        }
    }
    `

In a companion work, we outline various use cases of Jolt Atlas, including how it serves as guardrails in agentic commerce and for trustless AI context (often referred to as \textit{AI memory}).
Title: Jolt Atlas: Verifiable Inference via Lookup Arguments in Zero Knowledge
Authors: Wyatt Benno, Alberto Centelles, Antoine Douchet, Khalil Gibran
Date: Thu Feb 19 15:17:18 2026

We present Jolt Atlas, a zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) framework that extends the Jolt proving system to model inference. Unlike zkVMs (zero-knowledge virtual machines), which emulate CPU instruction execution, Jolt Atlas adapts Jolt's lookup-centric approach and applies it directly to ONNX tensor operations. The ONNX computational model eliminates the need for CPU registers and simplifies memory consistency verification. In addition, ONNX is an open-source, portable format, which makes it easy to share and deploy models across different frameworks, hardware platforms, and runtime environments without requiring framework-specific conversions. Our lookup arguments, which use sumcheck protocol, are well-suited for non-linear functions -- key building blocks in modern ML. We apply optimisations such as neural teleportation to reduce the size of lookup tables while preserving model accuracy, as well as several tensor-level verification optimisations detailed in this paper. We demonstrate that Jolt Atlas can prove model inference in memory-constrained environments -- a prover property commonly referred to as \textit{streaming}. Furthermore, we discuss how Jolt Atlas achieves zero-knowledge through the BlindFold technique, as introduced in Vega. In contrast to existing zkML frameworks, we show practical proving times for classification, embedding, automated reasoning, and small language models. Jolt Atlas enables cryptographic verification that can be run on-device, without specialised hardware. The resulting proofs are succinctly verifiable. This makes Jolt Atlas well-suited for privacy-centric and adversarial environments.
